newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia faces new shocks before recovery-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Serbia faces new shocks before recovery-analysts.

text.p: Serbia is bound for renewed economic crisis and devaluation before it undertakes genuine reforms and improves the investor appeal of Europe's last socialist state, analysts said on Wednesday.

"Serbia's economy is in a mess. However, there is a semblance of stability. Monetary policy is tight, interest rates are high and the dinar stable... But the core is rotting," David McWilliams of the BNP Eastern European Investment Banking Group told Reuters.
"This is a beer and froth analogy. Froth is nonsense and you want to blow all the froth off the beer to get to the beer," he said in an interview.

Deceptive stability masked the dual economy -- the official bankrupt and obsolete version and the more dynamic "grey" economy -- which buckled under the burden of massive deficits, BNP Eastern European Investment Banking Group said in its latest country report.

The country was blighted by huge trade, fiscal, employment and inter-company deficits and external debt vacuum, acting in malign harmony against any prospects of a sustainable economic recovery, the report said.

BNP analysts said Serbia needed urgently to restructure its inefficient state-sector, improve its credibility and increase productivity to support employment, generate tax revenue and make its exports competitive.

Any recovery will need to be export-led. But to do that, Serbia needs to attract cheap capital by boosting domestic productivity, giving tax breaks to foreign investors and maintaining a competitive exchange rate.
McWilliams insisted Serbia and Yugoslavia first needed to adapt the exchange rate of the overvalued dinar to economic realities.
The BNP study suggested the dinar was 33 percent overvalued against German mark. The dinar is officially fixed at 3.3 to the German mark, but BNP saw an equilibrium rate at 6.5 to the mark.
Other indicators suggested a general lack of faith in the Serbian economy, McWilliams said.

"All suggest fragile confidence and the froth is going to be blown off the beer in terms of devaluation. This will shock the government into acting properly, making Serbia open for foreign investment but in a proper way," McWilliams said.
Once the complexion of the economy has changed, Serbia will become more appealing to foreign investors and offer real value for invested capital.

"To attract demanding foreign investors, Serbia will have to become very cheap, very productive and make returns on equities very high," McWilliams said, adding he saw a brighter scenario in two or three years.
